Temporal Algebra¶

A Timeline stores instants on the nanosecond epoch axis. A Duration stores signed elapsed lengths. The operators preserve that distinction instead of treating both values as interchangeable integers.

Expression

Meaning

Result type

timeline + duration

move each instant by a signed elapsed length

Timeline

duration + timeline

the same shift with reversed operands

Timeline

timeline - duration

move each instant by the negated elapsed length

Timeline

timeline - timeline

measure signed elapsed distance

Duration

timeline relation timeline

compare paired instants

boolean Series

stream << timeline

write the public representation

std::ostream&

The operand types are part of the meaning. arrival - travel_time asks when a journey began and returns instants. arrival - departure asks how long the journey took and returns elapsed durations.

There is no implicit bare-integer timestamp arithmetic. An integer alone does not communicate whether its unit is nanoseconds, seconds, or days. Construct a Duration through an explicit unit factory such as nanos, seconds, minutes, hours, or days.

Shared Execution Contract¶

Arithmetic and comparisons are elementwise and rank-polymorphic. Operands align from the trailing axis, singleton axes may expand, and the result has the broadcast shape. A scalar has shape [], so it broadcasts across every lane of the other operand. Shapes [2, 1] and [1, 3], for example, produce [2, 3].

Every binary operation allocates a fresh contiguous result. +, binary -, and comparisons never rewrite their inputs. Compound assignment computes the same checked out-of-place result and then replaces the left-hand handle.

Arithmetic uses exact signed 64-bit nanoseconds. It does not pass through a floating-point representation. A result that would overflow the epoch range, the Duration range, or collide with the reserved NaT sentinel is rejected instead of wrapping.

A Timeline’s timezone controls wall-clock presentation, not the stored instant. Shift results retain the Timeline operand’s timezone. A Duration has no timezone. Timeline subtraction and comparison operate on epoch instants, so differently displayed values can compare equal when they identify the same instant.

Stream Insertion¶

operator<< writes the same public representation as pluss::timeline::print(...). It returns the stream, so normal stream chaining works. It is a presentation operation: it neither exposes the epoch buffer nor transfers ownership.

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});

std::cout << times << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-01 02:00:00 ]

Use epoch_nanos() when exact machine values are the subject of the output. Readable Timeline rendering intentionally does not expose every sub-second digit.

Addition¶

timeline + duration moves each defined instant later by a positive duration, earlier by a negative duration, and not at all by zero. The result timezone is copied from the Timeline operand.

duration + timeline is equally supported because elapsed displacement plus an instant is commutative. It reaches the same implementation and follows the same broadcasting, precision, absence, and overflow rules.

Scalar Shift¶

A rank-zero Timeline and rank-zero Duration produce a rank-zero Timeline.

const auto start = pluss::timeline::make("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
const auto shifted = start + pluss::duration::minutes(90);

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(shifted) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-01-01 01:30:00

Signed Values And Reversed Operands¶

The sign belongs to each Duration lane. Here the first instant moves later and the second moves earlier. Reversing the operands does not reverse direction, because both expressions are addition.

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
const auto offsets = pluss::duration::hours({1, -2});

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(times + offsets) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(offsets + times) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 01:00:00, 2024-01-01 00:00:00 ]

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 01:00:00, 2024-01-01 00:00:00 ]

Use whichever operand order makes the surrounding expression clearer. There is no semantic or performance distinction.

N-D Broadcasting¶

A [2, 1] Timeline can provide two day anchors while a [1, 3] Duration provides three intraday offsets. Pairing each anchor with every offset produces a [2, 3] Timeline.

const std::vector<std::string> values{
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-02T00:00:00Z"};
const auto anchors = pluss::timeline::make(values, {2, 1});
const auto offsets = pluss::duration::minutes({{0, 30, 60}});

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(anchors + offsets) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2, 3], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00 2024-01-01 00:30:00 2024-01-01 01:00:00 ]
[ 2024-01-02 00:00:00 2024-01-02 00:30:00 2024-01-02 01:00:00 ]

Broadcasting uses virtual singleton strides. It does not first materialize expanded copies of both operands.

Timeline Minus Duration¶

timeline - duration shifts instants by the negation of the Duration. A positive lane moves an instant earlier; a negative lane moves it later.

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
const auto offsets = pluss::duration::hours({1, -2});

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(times - offsets) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2023-12-31 23:00:00, 2024-01-01 04:00:00 ]

There is no duration - timeline overload. An elapsed length minus an epoch instant has no stable temporal result type. To measure elapsed distance, use a Timeline on both sides of -.

Timeline Minus Timeline¶

With two Timeline operands, subtraction measures elapsed distance and returns Duration. Each lane computes left_epoch_nanos - right_epoch_nanos.

  • Positive means the left instant is later.

  • Negative means the left instant is earlier.

  • Zero means both operands identify the same instant.

const auto left = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T03:30:00Z"});
const auto right = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
const auto elapsed = left - right;

std::cout << pluss::series::print(elapsed.total().seconds()) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 5400.0000]

The seconds projection is only for readable output. The returned Duration retains exact integer nanoseconds. Keep it as a Duration for further temporal arithmetic and project to a numeric unit only when the next calculation needs that unit.

This operator is the expression-oriented form of diff(). Both allocate a Duration, preserve broadcast shape, propagate absent lanes, and leave their Timeline operands unchanged.

Nanosecond Precision And Absence¶

Timeline arithmetic preserves every nanosecond. NaT is a reserved sentinel, not an ordinary early timestamp. If either paired Timeline or Duration lane is absent, the arithmetic result lane is absent.

The Timeline printer hides sub-second digits, so this example uses epoch_nanos() to make the exact seven-nanosecond shift visible. The second lane remains NaT instead of performing integer arithmetic on the sentinel.

const auto precise =
    pluss::timeline::from_epoch({100LL, pluss::Timeline::kNaT});
const auto shifted = precise + pluss::duration::nanos({7, 9});

std::cout << pluss::series::print(shifted.epoch_nanos()) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[107, -9223372036854775808]

Timeline-to-Timeline subtraction follows the same propagation rule and emits Duration::kNaT when either paired instant is absent.

Fixed Elapsed Time Across Clock Changes¶

A Duration is fixed elapsed time. Adding two hours always adds exactly 7,200,000,000,000 nanoseconds. It does not promise that a displayed local clock advances by two labels if its timezone changes offset in that interval.

The next instant displays as 01:30 before a spring clock change. Two elapsed hours later it displays as 04:30, because that local calendar skips the 02:00 hour. The result retains the Timeline’s timezone.

const auto local = pluss::timeline::make("2024-03-10T08:30:00Z")
                       .tz_convert("America/Edmonton");
const auto later = local + pluss::duration::hours(2);

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(later) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=America/Edmonton)
2024-03-10 04:30:00

Use Duration arithmetic when elapsed time is the requirement. Use named calendar transformations when the requirement is expressed as preserving or changing a wall-clock field.

Compound Assignment¶

+= and -= return Timeline&. They follow a checked replacement sequence:

  1. Validate and broadcast both operands.

  2. Compute a fresh Timeline through binary + or -.

  3. Replace the left-hand handle only after success.

  4. Return a reference to that left-hand object.

They do not write through the old epoch buffer lane by lane. Consequently, assigning through a copied handle does not rewrite the original handle.

const auto original = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
auto changed = original;

changed += pluss::duration::hours(1);
changed -= pluss::duration::minutes(30);

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(changed) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(original) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:30:00, 2024-01-01 02:30:00 ]

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-01-01 00:00:00, 2024-01-01 02:00:00 ]

Use binary arithmetic when both old and new values remain meaningful. Use compound assignment when the variable represents evolving state and its old value is no longer needed. A failed compound assignment leaves the left-hand Timeline unchanged because replacement happens only after validation and checked arithmetic succeed.

Comparison Operators¶

All comparisons are elementwise and return boolean Series; none collapses an entire Timeline to one C++ bool.

Operator

True for a defined pair when

==

both operands identify the same instant

!=

the operands identify different instants

<

the left instant occurs earlier

<=

the left instant occurs earlier or at the same instant

>

the left instant occurs later

>=

the left instant occurs later or at the same instant

The named methods eq(), ne(), lt(), le(), gt(), and ge() expose the same relations for method-oriented code.

Every Relation¶

The boundary below is scalar, so it broadcasts over the two-element Timeline.

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
const auto boundary = pluss::timeline::make("2024-01-01T02:00:00Z");

std::cout << pluss::series::print(times == boundary) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(times != boundary) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(times < boundary) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(times <= boundary) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(times > boundary) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(times >= boundary) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[true, true]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true]

When one answer is required, reduce explicitly. In this example one lane matches and one does not, so all() and any() answer different questions:

const auto left = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
const auto right = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T03:00:00Z"});
const auto matches = left == right;

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "all=" << matches.all().item<bool>()
          << ", any=" << matches.any().item<bool>() << '\n';

Output¶

all=false, any=true

Explicit reduction prevents a multi-element Timeline from acquiring an ambiguous truth value.

Higher-Rank Comparison Broadcasting¶

Here [2, 2] is compared with [2]. The row operand aligns with the matrix’s final axis and is reused for both rows.

const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::make({
    {"2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"},
    {"2024-01-02T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-02T02:00:00Z"},
});
const auto row = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T01:00:00Z", "2024-01-02T02:00:00Z"});

std::cout << pluss::series::print(matrix < row) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡  true  true ⎤
⎣ false false ⎦

Read the result after broadcasting: each matrix row is compared lane by lane with the same two row boundaries.

Timezones Compare Instants¶

Timezone conversion changes presentation while retaining the epoch instant. Therefore a UTC value compares equal to its converted local display.

const auto utc = pluss::timeline::make("2024-07-01T18:00:00Z");
const auto local = utc.tz_convert("America/Edmonton");

std::cout << pluss::series::print(utc == local) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=true

This is instant equality, not equality of timezone labels or displayed fields. Compare tz() explicitly if the metadata label is part of the condition.

Absent Instants Are Unordered¶

NaT follows an unordered absent-instant contract:

  • NaT == x is false, including when x is NaT.

  • NaT != x is true, including when x is NaT.

  • <, <=, >, and >= are false when either lane is NaT.

The second lane below is defined and equal to itself, making the contrast visible for every relation.

const auto values =
    pluss::timeline::make({"", "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"});

std::cout << pluss::series::print(values == values) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(values != values) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(values < values) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(values <= values) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(values > values) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(values >= values) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, false]

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true]

Prefer isvalid() or isnat() when validity itself is the question; those methods state the intent directly.

Building Interval Masks¶

Comparison results compose with Series logical operations. A closed interval includes both boundaries, so it uses >= and <= joined by logical_and().

const auto samples = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T01:00:00Z",
    "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T03:00:00Z"});
const auto start = pluss::timeline::make("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
const auto stop = pluss::timeline::make("2024-01-01T02:00:00Z");

const auto inside =
    (samples >= start).logical_and(samples <= stop);
std::cout << pluss::series::print(inside) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[true, true, true, false]

Use < stop for a half-open interval. Keeping boolean composition on the returned Series is why Timeline does not overload &, |, ^, or ~.

Empty Shapes¶

An empty broadcast is valid when the other operand contributes only compatible singleton axes. The result preserves its zero-length dimension and performs no lane reads. Empty shape is not scalar absence; the shape remains meaningful to later operations.

const std::vector<std::int64_t> no_ticks;
const std::vector<std::int64_t> shape{0, 2};
const auto empty = pluss::timeline::from_epoch(no_ticks, shape);
const auto boundary = pluss::timeline::make("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(
    empty + pluss::duration::hours(1)) << '\n';
std::cout << pluss::series::print(empty == boundary) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[0, 2], tz=UTC)

Series(shape=[0,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=0, contiguous=true)
[]

Failure Modes¶

Incompatible Shapes¶

Dimensions are compatible when equal or when either is 1. Otherwise the operation throws before producing a result. [2, 2] and [3] fail because their trailing dimensions are 2 and 3.

try {
  const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::make({
      {"2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T01:00:00Z"},
      {"2024-01-01T02:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T03:00:00Z"},
  });
  const auto three = pluss::timeline::make({
      "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-01-01T01:00:00Z",
      "2024-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
  (void)(matrix == three);
} catch (const std::exception&) {
  std::cout << "rejected: shapes do not broadcast\n";
}

Output¶

rejected: shapes do not broadcast

Arithmetic Overflow¶

The valid Timeline range reserves one signed 64-bit value for NaT. Addition, shift subtraction, and Timeline difference are checked independently. None can wrap to a plausible but incorrect instant or duration.

const auto latest = pluss::timeline::from_epoch(
    std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max());
const auto earliest = pluss::timeline::from_epoch(
    std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min() + 1);

try {
  (void)(latest + pluss::duration::nanos(1));
} catch (const std::exception&) {
  std::cout << "rejected: result is outside Timeline range\n";
}
try {
  (void)(earliest - pluss::duration::nanos(1));
} catch (const std::exception&) {
  std::cout << "rejected: result is outside Timeline range\n";
}
try {
  (void)(latest - earliest);
} catch (const std::exception&) {
  std::cout << "rejected: result is outside Duration range\n";
}

Output¶

rejected: result is outside Timeline range
rejected: result is outside Timeline range
rejected: result is outside Duration range

Deliberately Unsupported Operators¶

The absence of an overload is part of the contract. Operators that erase units, expose epoch encoding, or invent an arbitrary calendar step are intentionally unavailable.

Unsupported form

Why it is not Timeline algebra

Use instead

timeline + timeline

adding epoch origins does not produce an instant

subtract Timelines to measure distance

duration - timeline

elapsed length minus an instant has no temporal result

reorder the intended Timeline expression

timeline * x, timeline / x, timeline % x

scaling an instant is epoch-dependent

scale a Duration

unary +timeline, unary -timeline

reflecting around the epoch is not a date operation

project epoch values only when encoding is intended

++timeline, --timeline

no uniquely correct step exists

add an explicit Duration or use a calendar transform

timeline & timeline, `timeline

timeline, timeline ^ timeline, ~timeline`

bitwise operations expose storage rather than time semantics

timeline && timeline, `timeline

timeline, !timeline`

Multiplication and division may be meaningful for elapsed durations, but not for absolute instants. A fixed 24-hour Duration and a local calendar-day move also differ near clock changes. Requiring an explicit operation keeps the unit and temporal interpretation visible.

Ordinary copy and move assignment are standard C++ object mechanics rather than temporal operators. They copy or move a Timeline handle; only += and -= carry Timeline-specific arithmetic meaning.

Choosing The Right Form¶

  • Use timeline + duration or duration + timeline for fixed elapsed shifts.

  • Use timeline - duration for the opposite elapsed direction.

  • Use timeline - timeline for signed elapsed measurement.

  • Use comparisons for lane-wise temporal masks.

  • Reduce a comparison explicitly when one bool is required.

  • Use named calendar transformations when wall-clock fields must be preserved.

  • Use epoch_nanos() only when storage-scale integers are intentionally part of the next operation.
